sections.h2: What a New Jersey seller pays at closing
sections.html:
Expect one state fee, one possible state surcharge and a handful of private costs. The Realty Transfer Fee falls on the seller at recording, and the buyer owes none of it. No sales tax applies to a home sale. Private costs come from your contract and your lender, so they vary from deal to deal.

  • The Realty Transfer Fee, a rate applied to the price shown in the deed.
  • A graduated percent fee when the price tops $1,000,000.
  • Broker compensation, whatever your written agreement says.
  • An estimated income tax deposit if you live outside New Jersey and no exemption fits.
  • The mortgage payoff and any property tax still owed.

Most sellers also supply form RTF-1, the Affidavit of Consideration for Use by Seller. A deed that claims any exemption must carry that affidavit.

sections.h2: How the Realty Transfer Fee is calculated
sections.html:
The fee is stacked in slices: a dollar amount for each $500, at a higher rate for each higher slice of the price. It starts from the price stated in the deed. In a few situations the Division of Taxation substitutes assessed value divided by the Director's Ratio. Every deed that conveys title is covered unless an exemption fits.

Fee schedule for a standard sale priced above $350,000
Slice of the priceRate per $500
$0 to $150,000$2.90
$150,000 to $200,000$4.25
$200,000 to $550,000$4.80
$550,000 to $850,000$5.30
$850,000 to $1,000,000$5.80
Above $1,000,000$6.05

A cheaper schedule governs any sale at $350,000 or below, starting at $2.00 per $500 and topping out at $3.90. Qualifying seniors, blind or disabled persons and low and moderate income housing use reduced rates. The senior and disability reduction belongs to the person, so an estate or trust cannot claim it.

To see your own number, add up each slice of your price at its rate. Your closing attorney or title agent will run the exact figure, and you should ask for it before you set a net price.

sections.h2: The percent fee on sales above $1 million
sections.html:
This is a percentage of the full sale price, owed once consideration passes $1,000,000. Since P.L. 2025, c. 69 took effect on July 10, 2025, the seller pays it instead of the buyer. Older write-ups that call it a 1 percent buyer's mansion tax are out of date for deeds submitted on or after that date.

  • 1% of total consideration when the price runs from $1,000,000 up to $2,000,000.
  • 2% above $2,000,000 up to $2,500,000.
  • 2.5% above $2,500,000 up to $3,000,000.
  • 3% above $3,000,000 up to $3,500,000.
  • 3.5% on prices above $3,500,000.

Each rate applies to the entire price, so the cost jumps at every threshold instead of building slice by slice. A seller close to $2,000,000 or $2,500,000 should get the exact figure from the closing attorney before accepting an offer. The fee covers Class 2 residential property, farms with a residential building, Class 4A commercial property and cooperative units.

sections.h2: Deeds that escape the transfer fee
sections.html:
The Division lists a long set of full exemptions, and the seller claims one on form RTF-1. Check the facts closely, because each exemption is read narrowly.

  • Husband and wife, or parent and child, with adopted children counted and stepchildren left out.
  • An executor or administrator passing the house to a named devisee or legal heir.
  • Deeds for consideration under $100.
  • A deed whose only job is to confirm or fix one already on record.
  • Tax sale deeds and deeds on partition.
  • A deed between divorced spouses filed within 90 days after the decree.

Some transfers look exempt and are not. An executor who sells to someone not named in the will pays the fee. A will that orders a sale and a split of the cash is treated as a gift of money. Moving a house into a trust for other beneficiaries is taxable, and the terms of a divorce settlement agreement do not count as specific performance of a judgment. At a sheriff's sale, form RTF-8 is also required, and it is not an exemption.

sections.h2: Who sets broker compensation in New Jersey?
sections.html:
You and your brokerage do, in writing. Under P.L. 2024, c. 32, effective August 1, 2024, the brokerage must sign a brokerage services agreement with the seller in every residential transaction. It states the term, the amount of compensation and how it is calculated, and it must say that compensation is fully negotiable and not set by law (DOBI Bulletin 24-11).

  • Compensation can be a flat fee, a percentage of the price or another lawful method.
  • It can be paid by the seller, the buyer, a third party, or shared between brokerages.
  • The agreement must show whether the agency is exclusive or non-exclusive.
  • The brokerage must obtain a signed property condition disclosure statement from the seller.

Showings changed too. At a residential showing open to the public, agents must post a sign saying the agent represents the seller and that what a visitor tells the agent is not confidential. Read the agency section before you sign. New Jersey law recognizes seller's agents, buyer's agents, disclosed dual agents, designated agents and transaction brokers, and each owes you different duties.

The clerk of the county that contains the parcel records the deed. The package includes the RTF paperwork and a GIT/REP form, two separate requirements handed in at closing. Whether to accept the package is the clerk's decision.

If the package went to the wrong county, record it again in the right one. Form RTF-3 recovers the state share, and the county share needs a separate request to the office that took it by mistake. Have your title agent confirm the county before anything is mailed.

A little preparation keeps the closing day quiet. Ask the closing attorney or title agent for a written list of what comes out of your proceeds, and compare it to the items above: the Realty Transfer Fee, any percent fee, broker compensation, the mortgage payoff and unpaid property tax.

  • Bring your signed brokerage services agreement and the property condition disclosure statement.
  • Have the RTF-1 ready if any exemption is claimed on the deed.
  • Complete the right GIT/REP form. A seller living outside New Jersey also faces the estimated tax deposit, which is credited on the later tax return.
  • Ask for the mortgage payoff figure as of the closing date.

A cash buyer who takes the house as is removes lender appraisal and repair negotiations from the picture, but the state fees above still apply to the deed.

faqs.q: Which side of the table owes the transfer fee?
faqs.a: The seller does. It is collected at recording, and a buyer on an ordinary purchase owes none of it.

faqs.q: Does a house sale carry sales tax?
faqs.a: No. Home sales are outside sales tax in New Jersey.

faqs.q: What does the fee run on a $325,000 sale?
faqs.a: It runs $1,910 with no exemption, using the cheaper schedule for prices of $350,000 or below.

faqs.q: Does the old mansion tax still fall on buyers?
faqs.a: For deeds submitted on or after July 10, 2025, the seller owes the graduated percent fee on prices above $1,000,000. The rate starts at 1 percent and climbs to 3.5 percent.

faqs.q: Can I negotiate the real estate commission?
faqs.a: Yes. Broker compensation is fully negotiable, not set by law, and must appear in the brokerage services agreement.
